learningObjectives.title: Naked-eye and telescopic observation of the Moon

questions.q: What name is given to the large, dark, relatively flat plains on the Moon's surface?
questions.explain: Maria (Latin for 'seas') are the dark, smooth plains that appear as darker patches on the lunar disc.

questions.q: How were the lunar maria formed?
options: By ancient flows of basaltic lava filling large basins
By liquid water eroding the surface
questions.explain: The maria are solidified basaltic lava that flooded large impact basins early in the Moon's history.

questions.q: The bright, elevated regions of the Moon are known as the highlands, or by which alternative term?
questions.explain: The lunar highlands are also called the terrae, the brighter and more heavily cratered regions.

questions.q: What process is responsible for forming the vast majority of lunar craters?
questions.explain: Most lunar craters are impact craters produced when meteoroids and asteroids struck the surface.

questions.q: What does the name 'Mare Tranquillitatis' translate to in English?
questions.explain: Mare Tranquillitatis is Latin for the Sea of Tranquillity, the site of the Apollo 11 landing.

questions.q: Which statement best describes libration of the Moon?
options: A slow apparent oscillation that lets us view more than half the lunar surface over time
The regular cycle of the Moon's phases
The darkening of the Moon during a lunar eclipse
The Moon's steady change in distance from Earth
questions.explain: Libration is the apparent wobble of the Moon that reveals slightly more than one hemisphere over time.

questions.q: Owing to libration, approximately what percentage of the Moon's total surface can be observed from Earth over time?
questions.explain: Libration allows roughly 59% of the lunar surface to be seen from Earth, rather than just one half.

questions.q: What is the name for the line dividing the illuminated part of the Moon from the part in shadow?
questions.explain: The terminator is the boundary between the sunlit and dark portions of the lunar disc.

questions.q: Why do the lunar highlands appear brighter than the maria?
options: They are made of paler anorthosite rock, whereas the maria are dark basalt
They are permanently covered in water ice
They lie in permanent sunlight while maria are shadowed
They reflect light from the Earth
questions.explain: The highlands consist of light-coloured anorthosite, which reflects more light than the dark basaltic maria.

questions.q: Which region of the Moon is older and more heavily cratered?
questions.explain: The highlands are the older crust and are far more heavily cratered than the younger maria.

questions.q: What are the bright rays that radiate outwards from some craters?
options: Ejecta thrown out across the surface during the impact
questions.explain: Crater rays are bright ejecta blasted out and scattered across the surface during a high-energy impact.

questions.q: What causes libration in longitude?
options: The Moon rotates at a constant rate but travels at varying speed along its elliptical orbit
The tilt of the Moon's axis relative to its orbital plane
The daily rotation of the Earth carrying the observer
Changes in the Moon's distance alone
questions.explain: Because the Moon's spin is steady while its orbital speed varies, we glimpse slightly around its eastern and western limbs.

questions.q: Libration in latitude is caused by which of the following?
options: The tilt of the Moon's rotational axis relative to its orbital plane
The elliptical shape of the Moon's orbit
The rotation of the Earth during a night
The changing phase of the Moon
questions.explain: The axial tilt lets us see alternately a little beyond the Moon's north and south poles.

questions.q: Why does the Moon keep almost the same face turned towards the Earth?
options: Its rotation period is equal to its orbital period (synchronous rotation)
It does not rotate on its axis at all
It rotates exactly twice for each orbit
Earth's gravity has stopped it from spinning
questions.explain: Synchronous (tidally locked) rotation means one spin takes the same time as one orbit, keeping the same hemisphere facing Earth.

questions.q: Why are lunar craters seen most clearly when they lie near the terminator?
options: The low Sun angle casts long shadows that reveal relief and detail
The Moon is physically closest to Earth there
That region is the brightest part of the disc
The atmosphere is clearest along that line
questions.explain: Near the terminator the Sun is low, so long shadows pick out crater walls and mountains in sharp relief.

questions.q: Which lunar features are readily visible to the naked eye without a telescope?
options: The maria, seen as dark patches on the disc
questions.explain: The large dark maria are visible to the unaided eye, while fine detail such as small craters needs a telescope.

questions.q: An observer at first quarter wants to see craters with the sharpest, longest shadows. Where should they look?
options: At the centre of a large mare
questions.explain: Shadows are longest along the terminator, where the Sun is low, so features stand out most clearly there.

questions.q: An astronaut standing on the far side of the Moon looks around. What terrain would dominate their view?
options: Heavily cratered highlands with very few maria
Broad dark maria covering most of the surface
questions.explain: The far side is dominated by cratered highlands and has far fewer maria than the near side.

questions.q: Near new Moon you notice the unlit part of a thin crescent glowing faintly. What causes this glow?
options: Sunlight reflected from the Earth onto the Moon (Earthshine)
The Moon producing its own light
Light from a partial lunar eclipse
Starlight scattered by the lunar surface
questions.explain: Earthshine is sunlight reflected off the Earth that faintly illuminates the otherwise dark part of the Moon.

questions.q: Over a month an observer notices they can see slightly around the Moon's eastern and western edges at different times. Which type of libration is responsible?
questions.explain: Libration in longitude lets us peer a little around the east and west limbs as the Moon's orbital speed varies.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Astronomy (1AS0) specification; The Lunar Disc
